A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Generative Distribution Embeddings work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including material moved between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic reconstruction benchmarks, geometric analyses, and six biological applications, with numerical and qualitative results in the main text and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds Poisson estimation experiments, donor-level disease prediction, and an scVI comparison.

M1.justification: Section 3 changes the reported set-sampling rule from density ratios against the empirical label distribution to normalized densities against a fixed reference measure. v2 also adds partially labeled donor training combining reconstruction and disease prediction. The core encoder-generator framework is retained; the GNN-to-deep-sets terminology changes do not establish architectural replacements.

E1.justification: v2 adds donor-level prediction of six disease categories using a 4-million-cell subset of a human prefrontal-cortex atlas (Appendix B.3), and Poisson zero-event probability estimation (Section 5.1). These extend both population and task coverage. All earlier applications remain, including methylation, relocated to Appendix B.1.

E2.justification: v2 Table 4 adds scVI to the existing perturbation comparison. New comparisons include naive and Rao–Blackwellized Poisson estimators in Table 1 and a purely supervised donor encoder in Table 3. Existing synthetic and biological comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include donor learning with 10% labeled data and a reported 10% completely held-out evaluation, plus Poisson estimation across sample sizes 10–10,000 using one million generated samples. These accompany new experiments; the settings documented for retained experiments are unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.1 adds a sample-size analysis testing GDE estimation efficiency against naive and Rao–Blackwellized estimators. Existing architecture comparisons, prior-weighting sensitivity analyses, geometric interpolation studies, and biological case analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The five-trial mean ± s.e.m. synthetic results and ten-split viral evaluations retain their reporting practices. The new Poisson and donor tables provide point estimates without additional run counts, uncertainty intervals, or significance procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantive Poisson and donor prediction results. Table 1 shows GDE has the lowest Poisson MSE at n=10–1,000, but not 10,000. Table 3 reports semi-supervised versus supervised accuracy of 0.8887 versus 0.8791, ROC AUC of 0.5131 versus 0.4872, and F1 of 0.1479 versus 0.1293. Table 4 adds scVI R2=0.421491 and MSE=1.551414. Previously reported benchmark and biological results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 replaces the asymptotic Blackwell-equivalence argument with finite-sample sufficiency, minimality, and maximal-invariance results. D.2 strengthens regularity assumptions and qualifies loss-bias and generator-recovery guarantees. D.3 replaces total-variation reconstruction with bounded-Lipschitz reconstruction, adds smooth reconstruction assumptions, and rewrites the proof. Appendix C revises the Wasserstein manifold formalism and removes the Gaussian-mixture sufficient-statistics example; D.2 also corrects log-sum-exp normalization.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction now highlight donor-level representation learning in place of methylation among the six featured applications, although methylation remains in the appendix. The principal claims about distributional autoencoding, predictive sufficiency, and approximate Wasserstein geometry remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets GDEs as learned Rao–Blackwellizations and attributes their small-sample advantage to the meta-distributional prior. It more carefully distinguishes intrinsic manifold geometry from ambient Wasserstein geodesics and qualifies generator smoothness as a modeling assumption. The Discussion's existing limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 adds donor preprocessing, feature selection, architecture dimensions, joint training, and logistic-regression evaluation details. Section 2.2 and Appendix A.4 clarify training implementation, including using the generator's training loss without differentiating through sampling. The checklist adds configuration and notebook directory instructions; the repository link is unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on predictive sufficiency, cellular measurement noise, and the donor atlas, while removing several references associated with the earlier theoretical exposition. The statistical framing shifts toward classical sufficiency and Rao–Blackwellization. Positioning relative to kernel embeddings, Neural Statistician, and Wasserstein Wormhole remains essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: The methods section is substantially rewritten around a motivating example and a separate training subsection. Section 5 reorganizes the sufficiency and geometry narrative, incorporating the former prior-weighting subsection. Background and theory appendices are extensively rewritten, methylation moves to Appendix B.1, and implementation guidance, an expanded title, acknowledgements, and a NeurIPS checklist are added.

P2.justification: v2 adds a training algorithm display, Poisson and donor result tables, and an architecture overview table, and extends the perturbation table with an scVI row. Figure 2's panel descriptions are corrected, Figure 7's caption is clarified, and some figures are resized or relocated. Existing figure images are unchanged; appendix typography and table placement are adjusted.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is the repair of central theoretical weaknesses: Appendix D corrects the reversed TV/BL inequality, replaces total-variation reconstruction with qualified bounded-Lipschitz reconstruction, and explicitly requires correct specification for generator recovery. Clearer training guidance and additional experiments improve assessability. New results still lack uncertainty estimates, and Appendix A.5 contains stale cross-references, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in theoretical rigor and clarity.
